title: Rampartloom: using AI-assisted placeholder assets to test a 3v3 tower-wars game
author: Uzunn
selftext:
Hi, I’m Mumin, the developer of Rampartloom. I’m an architect and have played games for about 25 years. My friends and I used to play 3v3 Tropical Tower Wars, and those evenings inspired this project. I tried making another game before, but my limited coding knowledge made progress difficult.



Rampartloom combines tower-maze building with an income economy: you spend the same gold on defending your lane and on sending assault units to the opposing team. Sends increase your future income, so surviving an attack and keeping up economically can pull you in opposite directions. Teams share lives, and bots can fill empty slots when there aren’t enough players.



AI tools have assisted with parts of development, including some artwork, icons, 3D models, voices, sound effects and music. This is disclosed on Steam; no AI content is generated during gameplay. The current models and animations are test assets while I focus on the servers, multiplayer and gameplay. I’m planning a substantial model update and replacement of the animations.



One useful piece of feedback was that closely packed tower rows make it difficult for a new player to tell what each tower contributes. That is the next challenge for the visual work: having assets in the game lets me test the systems, but it does not automatically make a crowded match readable. I want the replacements to communicate tower roles and actions more clearly, as well as give the units personality.



There is a free Windows PC Steam Playtest if you’d like to see the current stage: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/5040240/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5040240/) — English, keyboard and mouse. I’m sharing my own game here, and it is still in development.



For developers who have moved from AI-assisted placeholders toward final visuals: how did you decide what to replace first when readability, rather than just visual polish, was the problem?
